passages.text:
In response, Simon said, “What else do I still have to say about the evil one except that God made him out of what did not exist? On this account the maker is evil: he made what did not exist come to exist, even though he could have made him good, since the being brought into existence possessed no nature of his own for choosing evil.”

Peter said, “Making him out of what did not exist, with a power of choice, is like the argument we stated earlier: by making his constitution such that he delights in evils, the maker himself appears responsible for what came into being. Since, then, both have a single solution, we will later discuss why he made him delight in the destruction of evil people.”

Simon said, “If he also made the angels with freedom of action, but the evil one departed from being righteous, why has he also been honored with rule? Through the honor he has given him, the one who honored him appears to delight in evils.”

Peter said, “If God appointed him, after he had rebelled, to rule over those like himself, ordering him to inflict punishment on sinners according to law, he is not unjust. But if the objection is that he honored him after he had rebelled, the one who honored him foresaw what was useful: both that the honor is temporary and that it is just for evil people to be ruled by an evil one and to be punished by him when they sin.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τὸν γενόμενον μηδὲν πρὸς κακίας προαίρεσιν ἰδίαν κεκτῆσθαι φύσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the being brought into existence possessed no nature of his own for choosing evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive supplies the ground for Simon’s assertion. μηδέν is taken with the possession of an independent nature, not as a restoration of the earlier phrase ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων. “Had no independent nature disposing him to choose evil” is a contextual alternative, but “disposing” is not made explicit in the Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ χαίρειν αὐτὸν κακοῖς τὴν κρᾶσιν ποιήσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: by making his constitution such that he delights in evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρᾶσις is the mixture or constitution of a being. “Temperament” would make the phrase more exclusively psychological. κακοῖς can mean evils or evil people; the following explicit reference to the destruction of evil people is rendered separately rather than supplied here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the destruction of evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive κακῶν is read as personal, in light of the subsequent punishment of sinners. “In the destruction of evils” remains grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with freedom of action
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective denotes having authority over oneself. “Self-determining” or “with free choice” are possible; the wording avoids importing a later fully developed doctrine of free will.

passages.text:
Simon said, “Could it be that he has always existed and thus overturns sole rule, with another power also ruling alongside it—the power associated with matter?”

Peter said, “If they differ in their substances, they also differ in their powers, and the stronger rules the weaker. But if they are of the same substance, then they are equal in power and alike good or evil. Yet they plainly are not equal in power, for matter was brought by the maker into whatever form of a world he wished. And surely one cannot say that it always existed as a substance, not as matter serving as God’s storehouse. For one cannot say, ‘There was ..... when God had no possessions.’ Rather, he was always its sole ruler. Therefore also eternal [μο........]; and on this assumption it could properly be spoken of, with both the ruler and the [........́.ου] existing.”

Simon said, “What, then? Did the evil one make himself? And is God good in this way: knowing that he would exist for evil, he did not destroy him as he came into being, when, being incomplete, he could have been destroyed? For if he came about suddenly, and fully developed at that, this is why he wages war against the maker, having suddenly become equal to him in power.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: sole rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The argument concerns the sole sovereignty of God, not a human political monarchy. “Single sovereignty” is another defensible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐσία οὖσα, οὐχ ὕλη ὡς θεοῦ ταμεῖον
lexical_decisions.chosen: as a substance, not as matter serving as God’s storehouse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative contrast is retained. οὐσία may mean essence or independently existing substance; the main text keeps the lexical distinction from ὕλη, matter. “Treasury” is an alternative for ταμεῖον.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he came about suddenly, and fully developed at that
lexical_decisions.rationale: συμβέβηκε presents coming about as an occurrence, without explicitly identifying a creator. τέλειος contrasts with ἀτελής, incomplete, earlier in the sentence.

source_issues.source_quote: Ἦν ..... ὅτε ἀκτήμων ἦν ὁ θεός
source_issues.issue: The edition prints a five-dot gap after “There was.” It is retained as exactly five dots. The missing content is not restored. “God had no possessions” renders the surviving ἀκτήμων, which can also mean propertyless.

The surviving fragment μο precedes an eight-dot printed gap. The English retains the fragment in Greek beside exactly eight dots, without completing it as “sole rule,” “monarchy,” or any other word. The preceding “eternal” translates surviving ἀίδιος; the incomplete syntax remains visible.

source_issues.source_quote: ὄντος καὶ τοῦ ἄρχοντος καὶ τοῦ ........́.ου
source_issues.issue: The final incomplete word consists of eight dots, an accent, one further dot, and ου. Its nine dots, accent and surviving ending are retained literally inside brackets. The construction introduces both the ruler and a second entity; the second entity is not identified by an invented restoration. The antecedent of “it could properly be spoken of” is affected by the earlier gap.

passages.text:
Peter said, “You are saying impossible things. For even while he was coming into being little by little, he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself. And, knowing beforehand that he would become not good, he would not have allowed it unless he knew that his coming into being would serve his own use. Nor was he capable of suddenly coming into being fully developed by himself, for someone who did not yet exist could not fashion himself. Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist. And one could not rightly say that something that has come into being is equal in power to what always exists.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, one of the things that are relative, and is it evil in this way? It is bad, for example, as water is to fire, but good for ground that is untimely thirsty. Iron likewise is good for farming but bad for murders; desire, too, is not bad for marriage but is harmful for adultery. So also killing is bad, but good for the killer in relation to what he has planned. And greed is bad, but pleasant for the greedy person. Everything of this sort follows this pattern. By this argument, neither is evil evil, nor is good good, for each produces the other. Does not what seems to be done evilly bring delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer? And if it seems unjust for someone who has loved himself to enjoy himself as much as possible, and because of this to suffer grievously at the hands of a righteous judge for having loved himself, to whom does it not appear unjust?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προαιρέσει ἀνελεῖν ἠδύνατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: God remains the understood subject of ἠδύνατο. προαιρέσει specifies choice, and ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ is represented reflexively as personal agency, “himself.” Another attachment is “as an enemy brought into being by him”; the Greek arrangement does not make the attachment entirely unambiguous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι τί οὐσίαν ἔχει δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject is taken as τί οὐσίαν ἔχει, “anything that has substance”; the negation is retained. This sentence is not harmonized with earlier competing claims about creation from nonexistence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one of the things that are relative
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός τι is the category of what is relative to something else; the supplied punctuation does not require a separate English clause. The following examples explicitly compare different effects on different recipients.

lexical_decisions.chosen: ground that is untimely thirsty
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκαίρως marks untimeliness or being out of season. “Ground thirsty at the wrong time” is an alternative; the adverb is not dropped as though the text merely said dry ground.

lexical_decisions.chosen: but is harmful for adultery
lexical_decisions.rationale: χαλεπή characterizes desire as difficult, harsh, or harmful in its adulterous use. “Troublesome” is possible but could understate the evaluative contrast.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ εἰ ἄδικον δοκεῖ τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπήσαντα. εὐφραίνειν ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο χαλεπὰ πείσεσθαι ὑπὸ δικαίου δικαστοῦ περὶ τοῦ ἑαυτὸν ἠγαπηκέναι, τίνι οὐκ ἄδικον φαίνεται;
source_issues.issue: The wording has a difficult scope for the first “unjust”: the articular infinitive and subsequent infinitive can gather the self-pleasuring and its punishment into a single stated situation. The main text retains both occurrences of “unjust” and the positive “loved himself” rather than supplying a missing negation or turning the opening adjective into “just.” Another reading would take the initial description of injustice as Simon’s concession before his challenge about punishment. The supplied punctuation after ἀγαπήσαντα is not treated as a completed sentence.

passages.text:
Peter said, “One must discipline oneself through self-control whenever desire wants to rush toward another person’s harm, knowing that the evil one can destroy evil people, having received authority against them from the beginning. And so this is evil for those who have done evil. But that their souls remain under punishment after their destruction—this is indeed grievous, with the one who said that the previously badly defined [one] was right speaking justly. For this reason, as I said, one must refuse to wrong someone else for the sake of a brief pleasure, so as not to bring oneself into everlasting punishment for the sake of a little pleasure.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, that there is nothing evil or good by nature, but the difference is a matter of law and custom ..̓̀.? Among Persians, marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice, whereas among others it is forbidden as something most grievous. Thus, since evils have not been defined for everyone, one cannot expect judgment from God.”

Peter said, “You cannot establish this. For it is apparent to everyone that having intercourse with mothers is abhorrent, even if Persians, who are one part of the whole, do not recognize the lawlessness of their abhorrent practice because of bad custom. So too Britons openly share with one another in front of everyone and feel no shame. Others eat human flesh and do not feel disgust, and others eat dogs’ flesh; still others do things that cannot be spoken of. Thus one must not make judgments by a perception that custom has diverted from what is natural. For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says that no one wants to experience it himself; and no one takes pleasure in theft when it means his own punishment. So even if in any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins, we must necessarily and rightly also expect a third judgment concerning those sins.”

After Peter said this, Simon replied, “Is this how matters concerning the evil one seem to you? Tell me.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: through self-control
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative specifies the means of disciplining oneself. “Restraint” is another direct rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bring oneself into everlasting punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀΐδιος explicitly conveys everlasting or eternal duration; the wording does not substitute “age-long,” and κολάσει is rendered punishment without making an additional claim about its purpose.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴδιον τὸ γαμεῖν μητέρας, ἀδελφάς, θυγατέρας
lexical_decisions.chosen: marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιον means peculiar or distinctive to the people named. The main text translates the ancient speaker’s assertion without independently endorsing the historical ethnographic claim or adding erotic description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς καὶ Βρεττανοὶ ἐμφανῶς ἐπὶ πάντων κοινωνοῦσι
lexical_decisions.chosen: So too Britons openly share with one another in front of everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοινωνοῦσι means participate or share; an object such as wives or sexual partners is not explicitly stated. The contextual implication is left to the reader rather than supplied as surviving source wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and others eat dogs’ flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preceding σάρκας…ἐσθίουσι supplies the ellipsis; κυνῶν is the genitive “of dogs.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: a third judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected source expressly has τρίτην, “third.” No change to “future judgment” or other conjectural reading is made, although the enumeration is not explained in this passage.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῦτο ὄντως εἶναι χαλεπὸν δικαίως τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον ὀρθῶς ἔχειν εἰπόντος
source_issues.issue: The main text is a deliberately close but unresolved representation. εἰπόντος introduces a speaker; τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον is masculine accusative, and ὀρθῶς ἔχειν can mean “be right” or “be in a right condition.” A possible construction is that the speaker said a previously badly defined argument was correct, with λόγον understood; another takes the masculine phrase as a person or being previously wrongly characterized. Neither the missing referent nor the identity of the genitive participle’s subject is explicit. The main text’s bracketed “[one]” exposes rather than silently supplies the missing referent. Independent source review must establish whether this is a defensible representation or whether a verified textual/grammatical clarification is required; it is not certified as resolved here.

The selected edition has two dots, accent marks, and a third dot after “custom.” The three dots and intervening marks are retained exactly as a printed gap; no conjunction or missing argument is supplied.

The square brackets mark supplied letters within words, not a dot-count lacuna. The supplied Greek is translated as printed (“forbidden as something most grievous”), and no additional conjectural letters are supplied.

source_issues.source_quote: κἂν οὖν ἑνὸς οὐδήποτε ὁμολογουμένου εἶναι ἁμαρτήματα
source_issues.issue: The construction is compressed: ἑνός is singular, while ἁμαρτήματα is plural, and οὐδήποτε is unusual in this position. “In any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins” takes ἑνός as one acknowledged instance and retains the plural sins. An alternative is “even if a single person anywhere acknowledges that there are sins.” The conclusion does not require specifying which referent of ἑνός is intended.

passages.text:
Peter said, “We remember that our Lord and teacher gave us this command: ‘Keep the mysteries for me and for the sons of my house.’ That is also why ‘he explained to his own disciples in private’ the mysteries of the kingdom of the heavens. But to tell the secret things to you, who fight against us and scrutinize nothing other than what is ours .... (whether true or false), is to act impiously. Yet, so that some of those standing here may not suppose that I am devising a pretext because I am unable to answer what you have said, I will speak, first asking you: if there were no suffering pain, what would the evil one still be?”

Simon said, “Nothing.”

Peter said, “Is evil, then, suffering pain and dying?”

Simon said, “It seems so.”

Peter said, “Then evil does not always exist; indeed, it cannot have existence. For suffering pain and dying are among the things that happen, neither of which occurs when sound health is present. For what is suffering pain other than something being out of harmony? And what is death other than the separation of a soul from a body? Thus there is no suffering pain when harmony exists. For dying is not even among things that have existence at all, because death is nothing, as I said, other than the separation of a soul from a body. When this occurs, the body, being naturally without perception, dissolves, but the soul, possessing perception, exists alive. Hence, when harmony exists, there is no suffering pain, no dying; nor indeed are there deadly plants, venomous creeping creatures, or anything else of this sort whose outcome is death. Hence, when immortality prevails, it will become apparent that everything has come into being with good reason. And this will indeed be so when the human being becomes immortal because of righteousness, with the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevailing, when his constitution too is well-balanced, so that not sharp ........ impulses; and his knowledge is also unerring, so that he may not [π.......] any of the evils as good; and he will be in pain, so that he may not be mortal.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ μυστήρια ἐμοὶ καὶ τοῖς υἱοῖς τοῦ οἴκου μου φυλάξατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: Keep the mysteries for me and for the sons of my house
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative recipients are retained as “for,” rather than converting the phrase into an unexpressed prohibition. “Preserve” is another rendering of φυλάξατε.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of the kingdom of the heavens
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural οὐρανῶν is retained without substituting an explanatory circumlocution such as God’s rule.

lexical_decisions.chosen: no suffering pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀλγεῖν concerns pain or suffering; “no suffering pain” preserves the experiential act rather than making it identical by definition with every moral evil. The subsequent ὁ πονηρός is rendered personally as “the evil one,” while τὸ πονηρόν is the abstract “evil.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: among the things that happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: This contrasts occurrences or events with τὰ ὑπαρκτά, things that have existence. “Accidents” has a possible technical philosophical sense but is less accessible and could mislead in ordinary English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ αἰσθητὴ οὖσα ζῶσα ὑπάρχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: but the soul, possessing perception, exists alive
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἰσθητή normally can denote perceptible, but here it contrasts the body’s ἀναίσθητον and supports a sense of having sensation. “Being perceptible” is the lexical alternative and is preserved here rather than treated as impossible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ χριστοῦ εἰρηνικῆς ἐπικρατούσης βασιλείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: with the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevailing
lexical_decisions.rationale: χριστοῦ is an independent title, so “Messiah” follows the supplied POB policy. The possessive and the adjective peaceful are retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his constitution too is well-balanced
lexical_decisions.rationale: The cognate words describe a well-mixed bodily constitution. The rendering is consistent with constitution for κρᾶσις in 19.16.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ ἡμέτερα .... (εἴτε ἀληθῆ ὄντα εἴτε ψευδῆ)
source_issues.issue: The four-dot gap after “what is ours” is preserved as exactly four dots. The source’s parenthetical true/false alternatives are retained; no missing purpose or verb is reconstructed.

The printed eight-dot gap is preserved as exactly eight dots. The surviving words are rendered as the visibly incomplete “so that not sharp ........ impulses.” No verb such as “experience,” “have,” or “feel” is invented for the missing text.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα μή τι τῶν κακῶν ὡς ἀγαθὸν π....... τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται, ἵνα μὴ θνητὸς ᾖ
source_issues.issue: The partial π and seven-dot gap are retained literally, with no conjectural verb. The surviving τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται is positive: “and he will be in pain.” The main text does not silently add “not” to harmonize it with surrounding claims of freedom from pain. The final “so that he may not be mortal” is retained. The loss could affect the attachment or scope of the surviving clauses; no claim is made to recover that lost syntax.
